prompt: Why is glass transparent? Essay please.

I've been reading about how the Romans made concrete that survives seawater for 2000 years while ours cracks in 50. Write an essay on what that says about how we define "better" materials. I don't want a chemistry lecture, more about the tradeoffs engineers are forced to make (speed of curing, cost, predictability) and whether we chose wrong.
Make the case that the slide rule taught engineers something calculators made them forget. ~1000 words, opinionated.

I'm a 34yo HVAC tech and my nephew asked me why heat pumps can move more heat than the electricity they use without breaking physics. I fumbled it. Could you write a short essay that explains it the way I wish I had, for a smart 16 year old who's skeptical of anything that sounds like a free lunch?
Write an essay examining why the second law of thermodynamics is the only fundamental law that seems to distinguish past from future, and whether that asymmetry is really in the physics or in us.

blog post idea: "the bridge that sang" — about the Tacoma Narrows collapse, but actually about how engineers learn mostly from failure and why that's uncomfortable to admit. casual tone, my readers are mostly software people

ok so this is kind of a weird one but I keep thinking about how every kitchen has a different relationship with salt? like chemically sodium chloride is boring, it's just an ionic crystal, but it does SO much: brining, curing, making bread rise slower, making ice colder. I want an essay that uses salt as a way into the idea that the most "boring" compounds are the most important ones. not a listicle. something with a through line.

I teach undergrad quantum mechanics. Every year students ask whether the wavefunction is "real" and every year I dodge it. Write an essay I could hand them that takes the question seriously without pretending it's settled. Assume they know the Schrodinger equation but not the philosophy literature. Around 1500 words.
Op-ed: cities should stop building glass skyscrapers. Thermal argument, mostly, but I'd like it to acknowledge why architects love them.
What I wish someone had told me about entropy before I spent four years being confused by it — write that essay.
Underrated: the humble bolt. Write about it.

I have a presentation for my materials science seminar next week and my professor wants a short reflective essay (800-1000 words) to go with it. My topic is why lithium-ion batteries catch fire and why it's so hard to engineer that risk away. I'm worried mine reads like a Wikipedia summary. Can you write a version that actually has an argument? Maybe something about how energy density and safety are basically the same property seen from two sides?
Write an essay arguing that the kettle is the most perfectly evolved appliance humans own, and use that to say something about when engineering should stop improving a thing.

Everyone says nuclear fusion is "always 30 years away." Is that actually a fair joke, or is it lazy? I'd like a balanced essay that looks at what's genuinely hard (plasma confinement, materials under neutron bombardment, tritium supply) versus what's just funding and politics.

Personal essay prompt: I grew up near a chemical plant in Louisiana and only as an adult understood what was coming out of the stacks. I'd like something in first person, about learning the chemistry of your own hometown. Feel free to invent details that feel true, but keep it grounded, no melodrama.

Compose an essay on why the color blue was so difficult for chemists to make, from Egyptian blue to YInMn blue in 2009, and what that difficulty reveals about the relationship between molecular structure and perception.
Why don't we have room-temperature superconductors yet?

My dad says modern cars are "built to fall apart" and old ones were tanks. I think crumple zones are the whole point. Can you write an essay that settles this, or at least makes it more interesting than our dinner-table argument?

Write an essay on the concept of tolerance in mechanical engineering (as in allowable deviation) and argue that it's one of the most philosophically interesting ideas in the field: the formal acknowledgment that perfection is neither possible nor desirable.
i just learned that GPS has to correct for both special AND general relativity or it'd drift ~10km a day!! write me an essay about how the weirdest physics ends up hiding inside the most mundane tech

Thesis to develop: "Recycling plastic is mostly a chemistry problem we've been pretending is a behavior problem." I'm thinking about the difference between thermoplastics and thermosets, the degradation each time you remelt, contamination, etc. Op-ed length, maybe 900 words, aimed at people who dutifully rinse their yogurt cups.
Why does ice float, and why is it such a strange stroke of luck that it does? Write it up as an essay for a general reader.

Write a piece for structural engineers on why redundancy is often treated as waste in value engineering reviews, and why that's a mistake. Use load path thinking. Don't explain basics, my audience has PEs.
Essay: the elegance of the transistor.

So I restore old mechanical watches as a hobby (have done maybe 40 by now), and there's this thing where a well-made escapement from 1920 keeps better time than you'd think possible given the tolerances they had. it got me thinking about precision vs accuracy and how humans managed to measure time before quartz. I'd love an essay that weaves the physics of the balance wheel and hairspring together with something bigger about patience and craft. don't make it too sentimental though, I hate that.

My mother was diagnosed with Alzheimer's two years ago, and I've been reading every headline about amyloid drugs. Write an essay about why the amyloid hypothesis has been so hard to abandon even as trial after trial disappointed. I want it honest, not cruel to researchers, and I'd like it to touch on what it's like to be a family member reading these headlines.
Argue that fever is underrated and we treat it too quickly. 800ish words.

Why do humans have such a long childhood compared to other primates? I'd like an essay exploring the competing explanations, especially the grandmother hypothesis, and whether any of them are fully convincing.
Write a blog post titled "Your Gut Is Not a Second Brain" pushing back on the overhype around the microbiome, while being fair about what's genuinely exciting in the research.

I'm a second-year med student and I'm honestly scared that I'm learning to see patients as lists of lab values. Can you write a reflective essay about the tension between the quantitative tools medicine relies on and the person in the bed? Not preachy please, I've read enough white-coat-ceremony speeches.
Write an essay on the evolutionary puzzle of menopause: why would natural selection favor a trait that ends reproduction decades before death?
what I wish I knew about running before I wrecked my knees at 22. essay form, personal voice, some physiology but mostly hard-won lessons

Op-ed arguing that antibiotic resistance is fundamentally an economics problem, not a science problem. The science of finding new antibiotics is hard but not impossible; the issue is nobody makes money on a drug you're supposed to use as little as possible. ~1000 words, for a general newspaper audience.
Write something exploring why octopuses are so smart despite living such short, lonely lives. Seems like a waste of a good brain, no?

I'm an epidemiologist. Write an essay for a lay audience about why "correlation is not causation" is a slogan that does more harm than good, because it teaches people to dismiss observational evidence entirely rather than think about confounding. Mention smoking and lung cancer as the obvious case where we never had an RCT.

My sister is a nurse and swears night shifts are slowly killing her. I'd like an essay on what circadian biology actually says about shift work, and what society owes the people who keep hospitals running at 3am.
Personal essay: being told at 41 that my cholesterol "isn't great" and realizing I'd been treating my body like a car I'd never get to trade in. Make it wry and honest, about 1200 words.
Write an essay considering whether the placebo effect should be thought of as a treatment in its own right, including open-label placebo studies, and what that would mean for informed consent.
Why do we get goosebumps from music? Write it up as an essay. I'm interested in the evolutionary weirdness of it, a leftover hair-raising reflex triggered by a chord change.

Every few months there's a new superfood or a new villain food (eggs, then butter, then seed oils). Write an essay on why nutrition science seems to flip-flop so much, and whether that's a failure of the science or of how it gets reported. I'm not looking for "it's complicated" as the conclusion.

Write an essay on CRISPR's origin story, how it came from people studying yogurt bacteria and obscure DNA repeats, as an argument for funding curiosity-driven research that has no obvious application.

I've been a vegetarian for 12 years and recently started eating fish again because my iron and B12 were tanking and honestly I feel a bit like a hypocrite. but it made me think about how much of what we call "natural" diet is really just a story about evolution we tell ourselves. could you write an essay about that? not about whether vegetarianism is right or wrong, more about how people (me included) use biology to justify choices they've already made for other reasons
An essay, please, on the history and ethics of the HeLa cell line, focusing less on the well-known story and more on what it should change about how we handle tissue donation today.
Why do cancers mostly come from the same few tissues? Write about it.
I want an op-ed arguing that hospitals should be designed around sleep. Patients get woken every 4 hours for vitals, alarms go off constantly, and recovery suffers. Punchy, around 700 words.
How does a single fertilized egg "know" how to become a hand with five fingers? Essay for a curious adult who hasn't taken biology since high school.

I donated a kidney to a stranger last year. People keep calling me a hero and it makes me squirm. Could you write an essay, in my voice, about why living organ donation is both less and more remarkable than people think? Some details: I'm 38, recovery took about 6 weeks, my remaining kidney has grown to compensate, and the recipient sent me one letter I've read maybe a hundred times.
Write an essay arguing that the 10,000 steps target is arbitrary, came from a pedometer marketing campaign, and that it's still a pretty good idea anyway.

Essay for clinicians: why the decline of the physical exam matters even when imaging is better at finding things. I'm an internist with 25 years in practice, so write with that authority and don't romanticize the old days.
Why are there no green mammals? Write an essay that starts with sloths and works outward.
